html:
The Hopewell tradition was a network of Native American peoples in the eastern woodlands of North America, from about 100 BCE to 500 CE. It was not one people or state. It was a set of communities along rivers in the Midwest and Northeast, joined by trade routes and by shared ways of burying and honouring the dead.

Its heartland was southern Ohio and the Illinois River valley. There people built huge earthworks: circles, squares and octagons of earth walls, some lined up with the rising and setting of the moon, such as the Newark Earthworks. They raised burial mounds over important people and filled them with fine goods.

Trade made Hopewell. Raw materials came from across the continent:

  • copper from Lake Superior
  • obsidian from the Yellowstone area
  • mica from the southern Appalachians
  • shells and shark teeth from the Gulf coast

Craftsmen turned these into ornaments, figures and stone platform pipes, which travelled far through local networks and turn up in graves well beyond the Midwest. At its widest the exchange ran from the north shore of Lake Ontario to the Crystal River mounds in Florida. It linked regional cultures such as Swift Creek, Marksville and the Goodall focus.

Hopewell grew out of the earlier Adena culture of the Ohio valley. After about 500 CE the great earthworks stopped being built, for reasons still argued over. Within a few centuries maize farming spread and the Mississippian towns rose. In 2023 eight Ohio earthworks became a World Heritage Site as the Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks.
